about.title: What we are learning today?
about.outcomesText: By the end of Phase F, students will be able to identify inverse functions, function composition, and function transformations to model real-world situations using appropriate functions (linear, quadratic, exponential).
objectives: Determine the concept of composition functions
indicators: Students can define function composition using the notation (f ∘ g)(x) or (g ∘ f)(x), and explain it using a real-world example with two sequential processes.
Students can determine (g ∘ f)(x) and (f ∘ g)(x) given two functions (linear, quadratic, or exponential), including finding an unknown function when the composite result is known.
Students can compare (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x) numerically and conclude that function composition is generally not commutative.
Students can translate a real-world situation into two functions, form the composite function, and use it to solve a contextual problem.

intro.text: Hey there! Welcome to my little corner of Cassava Valley. I've got fresh cassava straight from my field, and I want to show you how I turn it into crispy cassava chips. Come on, let me walk you through my two machines.

peeling-machine.text: This one right here is my Peeling Machine. Every time cassava goes in, the skin gets peeled off. No matter how much cassava I load in, about 15% of the weight is always lost to peel waste, which is just how much skin a cassava root naturally has.
peeling-machine.label: Peeling Machine

peeling-function.text: I call this process f, so:
peeling-function.formulaNote: where x is the weight of the cassava in kg.

washing-machine.text: And this one over here is my Washing Machine. After peeling, the cassava still has some sticky sap and dirt clinging to it, so I rinse it clean. Each time, it loses about 10% of its weight to water and rinsed-off starch, but there's also a little bit that always gets stuck in the machine's brush, about half a kilogram, no matter how much goes in.
washing-machine.label: Washing Machine

washing-function.text: I call this process g, so:
washing-function.formulaNote: where x is the weight of the cassava in kg.

machine-flow.text: Now here's the thing, I never use just one machine by itself. I always peel first, then wash. Let's say I've got 10 kg of cassava today. We'll find out!

quiz-peel.text: Let's say I load in 8,5 kg of cassava. After peeling, how many kilograms do I get?

quiz-wash.text: Nice, 7,225 kg is exactly right! Now that I've got 7,225 kg of peeled cassava, let's wash it. How many kilograms do I end up with after washing?

composition-explanation.text: See that? My cassava went through f first, then the result went through g. When two machines are used one after another like this, we call it function composition.

open-gof-machines.text: See how I calculated that in two separate steps? Let's make it faster. If I combine both machines into one formula, (g ∘ f)(x), what does it look like?

money-gross.text: Today I sold 20 kg of cassava chips. My exact price is Rp20.000 per kg, so before anything else, my gross earnings are Rp400.000.

money-intro.text: But of course, I give my customers a discount, and there's also a market retribution fee I have to pay. I always apply the discount first.

quiz-discount.text: If x is my gross earnings and I want to give my customer a 25% discount per kilos. Let's say discount as process f, what's the function of f(x)?
quiz-discount.explain: A 25% discount means the customer pays 75%, so f(x) = 0,75x.

quiz-retribution.text: Nice, f(x) = 0,75x is exactly right! Now I need to pay my retribution fees. It's about Rp80.000, so the function is...
quiz-retribution.explain: The fee is subtracted from the earnings: g(x) = x − 80.000.

open-gof-money.text: Good job! Now you know. Could you create a composite function based on that? I apply the discount first, then the retribution fee.

rafif-intro.text: You're doing well. So, let me introduce you to my friend, Rafif. He's also selling cassava chips just like me. Even though we use the same machines, there are some different things...

rafif-story.text: Hey, I'm Pak Rafif! Same day, same 20 kg, same Rp20.000 price per kg, so same Rp400.000 gross earnings as Pak Restu. Same discount, same retribution fee too. But I do it backwards. Retribution first, then discount.

open-fog-money.text: With that context in mind, please generate a composite function based on it.

open-restu-calc.text: How much is my final net income if my gross earnings today are Rp400,000?

open-rafif-calc.text: How about me, with today's gross earnings at Rp400,000, what would my final net income be?

open-difference-explanation.text: Now that you know their final net incomes, is there a difference between the two? Can you explain why?

open-conclusion.text: Based on the concept of composite functions, what conclusions can you draw regarding the net income of Pak Restu and Pak Rafif?

quiz-drag-experiment.text: Now, let's try a little experiment. You have two retribution options and two discount options. Match one retribution card and one discount card into the slots below—and remember, order matters! Try to find the combination that gives the highest net income for gross earnings x = Rp1.000.000.

dialogue-experiment-result.text: For x = Rp1.000.000, g₁(1.000.000) = 960.000, then f₂(960.000) = 0,95 × 960.000 = 912.000. This is the highest net income among all combinations — proof that choosing the right order is not just a math trick, but has a real financial impact.

eval-1.text: The Peeling Machine is f(x) = 0,85x and the Washing Machine is g(x) = 0,9x − 0,5. Pak Restu always peels first, then washes. For 10 kg of cassava, what is (g ∘ f)(10)?

eval-2.text: Using the same machines as Question 1, Pak Rafif washes first, then peels. What is (f ∘ g)(10)?

eval-3.text: Pak Restu's gross earnings are x = Rp1.000.000. With f(x) = x − 60.000 (retribution) and g(x) = 0,9x (discount), applying retribution first then discount, what is the final amount?

eval-4.text: The Frying Machine is f(x) = 0,8x and the Seasoning Machine is g(x) = x² + 2x. Pak Restu seasons first, then fries. For x = 4 kg of cassava, what is f(g(4))?

eval-5.text: Comparing retribution-first-discount versus discount-first-retribution (using f(x) = x − 60.000 and g(x) = 0,9x from Question 3, starting from x = Rp1.000.000), which order gives Pak Restu the higher final amount, and what is the difference?
eval-5.explain: Retribution first: (g ∘ f)(1.000.000) = 0,9 × 940.000 = Rp846.000. Discount first: (f ∘ g)(1.000.000) = (0,9 × 1.000.000) − 60.000 = Rp840.000. Retribution first is higher by Rp6.000.
options: Both orders give the same amount
